observations.text: SP, due to an incomplete wind-correction technique, did not apply a timely heading correction to regain the planned ground track after the first turning point, with the result of a lateral displacement beyond 2 NM. The IP had to direct the correcting heading and to perform part of the map-to-ground orientation. Further practice in dead-reckoning track control is required.

SP, due to lack of awareness of the aircraft's position relative to the planned route, did not maintain orientation during navigation and did not recognize the developing offset, with the result of a displacement of about 3 NM from the planned ground track. The IP directed the return to course and recalculated the remaining flight time. Renewed emphasis on continuous position awareness is required.

SP maintained the planned ground track within the standards of the Training Section; however, displacement reached 2 NM before the correction was started, and the return to course was completed after the IP's verbal prompts. Wind effect was recognized only on the second leg, so the update of flight time and fuel was made with delay. Marginal performance for this stage - earlier recognition of track deviation is expected to improve.

SP applied appropriate procedures and techniques to maintain the planned ground track and corrected each deviation as soon as practical, without IP's intervention. Displacement did not exceed 1.5 NM on any leg, and wind effect was assessed in flight and used to update the estimated leg times. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP maintained the planned ground track accurately throughout the route, keeping displacement within 1 NM on every leg. Wind effect was recognized in flight and flight time and fuel were recalculated without prompting, with orientation maintained at all turning points. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP maintained the planned ground track with negligible deviations, no leg exceeding 0.3 NM of displacement, and every turning point was crossed on the planned course and on time. Drift was quantified on the first leg and applied thereafter as a standing correction, with flight time and fuel recalculated ahead of the IP's request. Orientation was maintained continuously and the accuracy demonstrated was above the desired levels. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to a non-standardized map-to-ground orientation technique, did not identify the drift developing on the second leg and applied no correction to regain the planned ground track, with the result of a displacement of about 3.5 NM. The IP took over the navigation task and directed the intercept back to course. Additional ground practice on dead-reckoning corrections is required.

SP, due to acceptance of the automated navigation solution without an independent check against the chart, did not maintain the planned ground track and did not detect that the active leg differed from the planned route, with the result of a displacement in excess of 2.5 NM. The IP directed the return to the planned track and recalculated the remaining flight time and fuel. Cross-check of the automated presentation against dead reckoning is required.

SP, due to a late and undersized heading correction, did not correct the track deviation as soon as practical, with the result that displacement reached 2 NM before the aircraft was returned to the planned ground track. The correction was completed only after the IP's verbal prompt, and the error was recognized with delay.

SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated the radio work and the chart study inside the same leg, did not monitor the accumulating drift and did not correct the track deviation as soon as practical, with the result of a 2 NM displacement at the limit of the standard. Return to the planned ground track and the update of the leg time were completed only after the IP's verbal prompts, with delayed recognition of the wind effect.

SP maintained the planned ground track within the desired standards; however, displacement twice approached 1.8 NM before the correcting heading was applied. Deviations were recognized and corrected in a timely manner without IP's intervention, and wind effect was assessed only from the third leg onward. Marginal performance for the Training Section - earlier detection of drift is expected to improve.

SP used all appropriate procedures and techniques to maintain the planned ground track, correcting every deviation as soon as practical and without IP's intervention, with displacement kept within 1 NM throughout the route. Wind effect was recognized in flight, flight time and fuel were recalculated accurately, and orientation was maintained at every turning point. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP maintained the planned ground track with negligible deviations, no leg exceeding 0.3 NM of displacement, and every turning point was crossed on course. Drift was quantified on the first leg and applied thereafter as a standing correction, with flight time and fuel recalculated without prompting. Orientation was maintained continuously and the accuracy demonstrated was above the desired levels. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to an incorrect application of the computed drift correction, turned onto a heading that increased rather than reduced the offset from the planned ground track, with the result of a displacement in excess of 3 NM and loss of orientation on that leg. The IP had to direct the recovery to course and to establish the position by reference to a major landmark. Review of the wind-correction computation is required.

SP, due to continuation of the briefed heading after the observed ground features no longer matched the chart, did not reassess the position and did not correct the track deviation, with the result of a displacement of about 4 NM and an unrecognized error in the estimated time to the turning point. The IP intervened to re-establish orientation and directed the return to the planned ground track. Timely inquiry when the observed picture does not match the plan is required.

SP, due to a coarse heading-holding technique between turning points, did not maintain the planned ground track and did not correct the developing offset as soon as practical, with the result that displacement reached 2 NM. The track was regained only after the IP's verbal prompt, and the recalculation of the leg time was made with delay.

SP, due to an interrupted cross-check of the heading indicator while attention remained on the chart, did not maintain the planned ground track and recognized the offset only when it had reached 2 NM. Correction and the associated update of flight time were completed after the IP's verbal prompts, so recognition and correction were achieved with delay.

SP, due to a heading correction applied without allowance for the drift already computed, did not regain the planned ground track at the first attempt, with the result of a maximum displacement of 1.5 NM on the second leg. The deviation was recognized and corrected in a timely manner, without IP's intervention.

SP, due to distraction by the fuel check carried out inside the turn, did not begin the correction of the track deviation as soon as practical, with the result of a displacement of 1.6 NM before the aircraft was returned to the planned ground track. Wind effect was reassessed and the leg time updated by the SP, without IP's intervention.

SP maintained the planned ground track within the desired standards, with displacement not exceeding 0.9 NM on any leg. Corrections were applied without IP's intervention; however, they were initiated only once the offset had become apparent on the chart, rather than from the heading and time computation. Marginal performance for this stage - anticipation of drift and earlier correction are expected to improve.

SP maintained the planned ground track with negligible deviations, no leg exceeding 0.3 NM of displacement, and all turning points were crossed on course and within the estimated times. Wind effect was quantified on the first leg and applied thereafter, with flight time and fuel recalculated accurately and passed to the IP without prompting. Orientation was maintained continuously throughout the route. Above end of block MIF achieved.
